title: Rabbi Yose son of Rabbi Yehudah (a Tanna of the Mishnah)
author: Aharon Hyman

paragraphs: Rabbi Yose son of Rabbi Yehudah. (A Tanna of the Mishnah.) He was the precious son of Rabbi Yehudah (without further designation) bar Ilai, as stated explicitly in Nedarim 8:6: “Rabbi Yehudah says … Rabbi Yose his son says.” In Bava Kamma 85a: a dispute of Rabbi Yehudah and the sages, and afterward Rabbi Yose son of Rabbi Yehudah, and they said there that he holds like his father; and so it is in Menachot 63b. Without doubt, in Hyman’s view, he received his Torah from his father, and as above,

he holds like his father; likewise in the Jerusalem Talmud, Eruvin, end of chapter 1, they said: “Rabbi Yose son of Rabbi Yehudah’s [view] accords with his father’s method.” In Jerusalem Talmud Maaserot 3:1: Rabbi and Rabbi Yose son of Rabbi Yehudah were bringing the basket in behind the roofs; Rabbi Yehudah bar Ilai saw them and said to them, “See what [a difference] there is between you and the early ones,” etc. Likewise we find that he spoke in the name of Rabbi Eliezer,

as in Pesachim 94b and Sotah 2b, and in the name of Rabbi Zekharyah ben HaKatzav, as in Bava Batra 111a; but Hyman argues that they were not his teachers, for they lived two generations before him. Seder HaDorot cites Tosefta Bekhorot, chapter 7: “Three threshing times for the animal tithe: at the peras before Passover [the supplied transcription reads פרם; see notes] … the words of Rabbi Akiva; Rabbi Yose son of Rabbi Yehudah says … Ben Azzai said,” etc. Hyman wonders that a Gaon like the author of Seder HaDorot could think that he

disagrees with Rabbi Akiva and Ben Azzai, and reckons Ben Azzai as the latest of them. He did not examine there that the Tosefta gives briefly what is explained at length in Bekhorot 57b–58a, for there Rabbi Akiva’s words are cited in the Mishnah, and in the baraita Rabbi Yose son of Rabbi Yehudah comes to explain Rabbi Akiva’s words — what the term peras means [the supplied transcription reads פרם here] — and says that a peras is not less than fifteen days; and Ben Azzai’s words do not refer to their words at all, but to the words of Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Shimon. And the Gemara asks:

How could Ben Azzai speak about their words — was he not greater than all the sages of the generation? And it answers that they said this from the mouth of Haggai, Zechariah and Malachi. Hyman considers this clear; and in the Tosefta the matter is cited briefly. In Jerusalem Talmud Megillah 1:1 he asked Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha. Rabbi Yose son of Rabbi Yehudah is mentioned in the Mishnah: Eruvin

1:10; Pesachim 4:6 (some versions have Rabbi Yehudah there); Nedarim 8:6; Gittin 4:7; Bava Metzia 7:3; Sanhedrin 8:3; Makkot 2:6; Zevachim, beginning of chapter 6; Menachot, end of chapter 8; Chullin 1:3; Bekhorot 9:7; and Temurah 2:3. Seder HaDorot counts that he is mentioned in Sotah 9:9; Hyman identifies this as an error, for there it lists the pairs: Yose

ben Yoezer and Yose ben Yochanan, and through a printing error it reads Yose ben Yehudah. His well-known halakhot: Shabbat 5a: “If he stuck a reed in the public domain with a basket on its top, and threw [something] onto it, he is liable.” There, 117b: “If his jug broke on Shabbat, one may use a stratagem to save [its contents].” Eruvin 1:10: “Any partition that is not

of warp and woof is not a partition.” Eruvin 30b: “One who enters the land of the nations in a chest, box or cupboard — he declares him pure” (for he holds that a moving tent is called a tent). Pesachim 7a: “We follow the majority.” There, 39b: “Flour into which a drip falls, even all day long, does not come to leavening.” Yoma 85b: “‘But you shall keep My Sabbaths’ —

I might think in all [cases]; the verse says ‘but’ — to distinguish.” There, 88a: “Sufficient for the immersion that it be at the end” (for he holds that immersion at its proper time is not a mitzvah). Hyman cites Sukkah 56b for “The flute overrides Shabbat.” At Sukkah 51a: “The song of the [water] drawing overrides the Shabbat.” Nedarim 76b: annulment of vows [is valid] for twenty-four hours. Kiddushin 21a: he expounds inclusion, exclusion and inclusion.

Bava Metzia 7:3: that (a worker) does not eat until he works with his hands and feet. Sanhedrin 8b: a chaver [a scholar presumed to know the law] does not require a warning. Chullin 1:3: “[If a thread-breadth remains] over most of the [windpipe’s] ring”; and in the Gemara there, 18a: even though they do not encircle the entire windpipe, his slaughter is valid. There, 43a: a perforation of the gall bladder renders it terefah. Menachot 84a: the omer may come from outside the Land, and new grain is forbidden

outside the Land by Torah law. Arakhin 20a: if he said, “Half my valuation upon me,” he pays a full valuation. In aggadah we find his precious sayings: Shabbat 119b, where he said: “Two ministering angels accompany a person on Shabbat eve from the synagogue to his home. When he comes home and finds a lamp lit and a table set … the good angel says: May it be [God’s] will that it be so for another Shabbat,

and the evil angel answers Amen against his will; and if not, the evil angel,” etc. In Taanit 9a: “Three good leaders arose for Israel: Moses, Aaron and Miriam.” In Bava Metzia 49a: “What does the verse teach, ‘a just hin’? — that your ‘yes’ should be just and your ‘no’ just.” His great colleagues: He was the great colleague of our holy Rabbi,

and Hyman considers it undoubted that both studied with Rabbi Yehudah, as we find their disputes in Shabbat 18a and 87a, Eruvin 30b, Sukkah 50b, Chagigah 24b, Kiddushin 21a, Sanhedrin 8a and Tosefta Temurah, chapter 4. We find both together, as in Nedarim 62a: “Rabbi and Rabbi Yose son of Rabbi Yehudah came to a certain place.” In Jerusalem Talmud Sheviit 6:4, both went down to Akko and were received by Rabbi Mana (he is Rabbi Muna the Tanna,

Rabbi Yehudah’s student). In Sifrei, Haazinu, on “And he said to them”: an incident in which our master came from Laodicea, and Rabbi Yose son of Rabbi Yehudah and Rabbi Elazar ben Yehudah came in and sat before him. Hyman explains that he was so great in the eyes of Rabbi and the sages of the generation that sometimes Rabbi set down the anonymous Mishnah according to him; therefore Rabbi Yose son of Rabbi Yehudah is called setimta [an authority behind an anonymous teaching], as in Eruvin 38b and Bekhorot 51a. In three places

we find that they said in the Gemara of Rabbi Yose without further designation that he is Rabbi Yose son of Rabbi Yehudah: Shabbat 121a, the end of Yoma, and Makkot 6b. We likewise find in Beitzah 35b that he disagrees with Rabbi Yaakov; in Bava Batra 111a and Yevamot 101b he disagrees with Rabbi Elazar son of Rabbi Yose; in Nedarim 76b he disagrees with Rabbi Elazar son of Rabbi Shimon; in Shabbat 136a, Shevuot 19b and Keritot 18b both agree; and in Yoma

85b he disagrees with Rabbi Yonatan bar Yosef and Rabbi Shimon ben Menasya. Hyman infers that he died before Rabbi, as we find in Pesachim 112b: “Rabbi Yose son of Rabbi Yehudah commanded Rabbi three things: Do not go out alone at night, do not stand naked before a lamp, and do not enter a new bathhouse.” And what we find in Tanchuma, Chukkat 21, “Rabbi Idi

and Rabbi Huna in the name of Rabbi Yose son of Rabbi Yehudah in the name of Shmuel,” Hyman identifies as a scribal error and says the reading should be “Rabbi Huna in the name of Rav Yosef in the name of Rav Yehudah.” He is mentioned in the Zohar, Chayei Sarah, in the Tosefta, 123b, with Rabbi Chiyya. Hyman reports finding no student of his and explains this by the great part he took in arranging the Mishnah while sitting with Rabbi, and therefore all were counted as Rabbi’s students; as we explained in his entry, in Rabbi’s days

all private academies were abolished, and all were subordinate to Rabbi’s great assembly house, in order to bring forth the wonderful undertaking to the light; and this was with the help and counsel of all the sages of the generation.

notes.text: This scan-derived notice preserves complete printed L-group portions and their cross-unit continuations. הבירו/ובל״ם are interpreted as חבירו/ובל״ס, and מע״ל as a twenty-four-hour period. The supplied פרם in the Passover/peras discussion is interpreted provisionally as פרס, as Hyman’s own later spelling and saved DavidsonBekhorot58a’s fifteen-day statement support; the exact supplied-letter question remains held, with no claim about printed pixels or how it arose. Fable’s latest-of-them correction describes what Hyman criticizes Heilprin for reckoning, not an instruction to count BenAzzai last. Hyman’s objections to SederHaDorot and school/generation/conjectural teacher relationships retain his voice and original force, without altering Heilprin or merging authorities. Source Sukkahנו:56b remains alongside the saved50b flute ruling; the saved56b ending scalar is a bounded nonmatch, not printed-source proof. This locator discrepancy remains a source question. Chullin1:3’s חוט is a remaining THREAD-BREADTH of the tracheal cartilage RING, not a cut thread of a plant reed; ToratEmetMishnah1:3 and Davidson18a–18b supply the connected anatomy. The baraita’s incomplete rings still encircle most of the WINDPIPE. Bekhorot58a directly supports fifteen days; its later dispute includes RabbiElazar together with RabbiShimon, alongside Hyman’s abridged Meir-and-Shimon formulation. Nothing is silently inserted into Hyman’s text. The proposed Tanchuma chain correction, death-before-Rabbi inference and explanation of no named students remain Hyman’s assertions. All source questions supplied by Fable remain recorded.

Here setimta describes the sage associated with an anonymous teaching, as Hyman immediately explains by Rabbi’s setting down the Mishnah according to his view; it does not mean that this named sage’s identity is unknown.

The consulted editions preserve occurrence-specific forms rather than establish a single harmonized chain or chronology. Mishnah Nedarim 8:5 names Rabbi Yehudah and 8:6 says “Rabbi Yose his son”; Bava Kamma 85a offers alternative explanations, one comparing the son's view with his father's, and Menachot 63b explicitly asks how his position differs from his father's. Hyman's certainty that his father taught him remains Hyman's inference. Jerusalem Talmud Eruvin 1:10 says that his view both follows and differs from his father's. The attempted Maaserot 3:1 retrieval did not provide a witness for comparison. Pesachim 94b and Sotah 2b explicitly transmit in Rabbi Eliezer's name; Bava Batra 111a gives Rabbi Yose son of Rabbi Yehudah together with Rabbi Elazar son of Rabbi Yose in Rabbi Zekharyah ben HaKatzav's name. These attestations do not independently establish the personal teacher relationships Hyman infers.

Bekhorot 57b–58a and Tosefta Bekhorot 7 support the festival periods and fifteen-day explanation, while the supplied פרם and Hyman's later פרס remain as supplied. His criticism of Heilprin's reckoning of Ben Azzai is retained as his criticism, without adopting its chronology. The checked opening discussion of Jerusalem Talmud Megillah 1:1 does not establish the intended comparison. Mishnah Pesachim 4:6 has Rabbi Yose bar Yehudah in the consulted edition; Hyman's report about other printings is not a fresh collation. Mishnah Sotah 9:9 does not supply the reported pairing in the checked text. The cited Mishnah occurrences otherwise retain their own titles and patronymics.

Sukkah 50b explicitly gives the flute ruling and 51a discusses the competing explanations about sacrificial song and the water-drawing celebration, beside Hyman's literal 56b reference. Arakhin 20a first says “is penalized and gives a full valuation,” then immediately explains the penalty as liability for the full valuation; it does not justify adding a corporal punishment to this translation. Shabbat 119b, Taanit 9a, and Bava Metzia 49a attest the quoted sayings. Rashi on Eruvin 38b explains setimta as someone whose views Rabbi repeatedly taught anonymously in the Mishnah; Eruvin also preserves an alternative list omitting Rabbi Yose. The checked Bekhorot 51a passage names Rabbi Yose and Rabbi in a dispute, without independently establishing Hyman's entire editorial history.

Sifrei Devarim 335 gives the Laodicea visit, and Jerusalem Talmud Sheviit 6:4 gives Rabbi and Rabbi Yose son of Rabbi Yehudah visiting Rabbi Mana in Akko; Hyman's Mana/Muna identification and general teacher inference remain attributed. Pesachim 112b explicitly gives the three instructions to Rabbi. The collections differ in their pairings: Shabbat 136a and Nedarim 76b name Rabbi Elazar son of Rabbi Shimon; Yevamot 101b names Rabbi Elazar son of Rabbi Yose; Shevuot 19b has Rabbi Shimon son of Yehudah, while the consulted Keritot 18b reads Rabbi Yose son of Rabbi Yehudah, Rabbi Elazar, and Rabbi Shimon. Hyman's forms and locators are retained alongside these differences. The checked Kiddushin 21a page does not establish the intended occurrence; 21b positively attests Rabbi Yose's dispute with Rabbi.

The consulted standard Tanchuma Chukat 21 section did not match the reported transmission chain, and the attempted Zohar locator did not return a text for comparison. Hyman's assertion of a scribal error and his statement of what SHOULD READ remain his proposed correction, not a change to the Hebrew or an independently verified chain. His generation gap, death-before-Rabbi argument, school-consolidation explanation, absence-of-students assertion, and exhaustive or printing-history claims remain his reports and inferences. No witness census, printed-glyph verification, identity merger, or silent locator correction is claimed; the supplied-letter and locator questions remain unresolved.

The earlier notes record the state of the evidence before this printed page and the parallel passages were checked. In the supplied Hebrew, the first two occurrences end in final mem (פרם) and the third has samekh (פרס). The near-identical shapes in the scan of Hyman, vol. II, p. 727, leave the precise letters uncertain. The consulted Tosefta Bekhorot 7:6 reads בפרס הפסח and gives Rabbi Yose’s explanation as at least fifteen days before the festival, as does Bekhorot 58a. That establishes the sense of peras here. In Bekhorot 58a the discussion of Ben Azzai and Rabbi Akiva on the Passover gathering date is separate from the later debate about tithing animals born in Elul, which names Rabbi Meir and the pair Rabbi Elazar and Rabbi Shimon. Hyman is criticizing Heilprin’s reckoning of Ben Azzai as the latest authority.

Hyman, vol. II, p. 727, visibly prints Sukkah נו: (56b) beside the flute ruling. In the consulted text, Sukkah 50b attributes “The flute overrides Shabbat” to Rabbi Yose bar Yehudah, and the Sages disagree. Sukkah 51a separately gives the debate about the song of the water-drawing and distinguishes it from the song accompanying an offering. The supplied 56b is retained as Hyman’s locator.
